section per domain, such as `api.tasks.getTask(key)` or
`api.images.listImages()`. The target is fixed when the client is created:
`undefined` resolves to the active host once, and a later host switch never
redirects an existing client. A registered host without an endpoint (an SSH
tunnel that is reconnecting) yields a client whose `ready` is false; its
requests fail with `host_not_ready` and never fall back to the local daemon.

React code reads the client from context:

~~~tsx
const api = useApi()
const detail = await api.tasks.getTask(taskKey, signal)
~~~

`ApiProvider` fixes the server for the tree below it. `DaemonProvider`
provides the active host, `RouteHostBoundary` provides the route host, and
an agent workspace, a server pane, or a dialog with its own host picker mounts
a provider for that host. Components do not pass a target down to children.
`useApi()` outside a provider throws, and component tests render through
`@/test/queryRender` or the `apiWrapper` / `fakeApi` helpers in
`@/test/api.tsx`. An equal target keeps the same client across renders, so
effects and subscriptions that depend on `api` do not restart. A new endpoint
or token for the same host gives a new client without changing any tree key:
loaded data and unsaved drafts survive a reconnect, while requests and
subscriptions move to the new connection. A response from the previous client
never replaces data of the current one.

Code that works with several hosts at once creates one client per host with
`createApi(daemon)`: the all-hosts agent list, the all-servers task view, and
customer question notifications. A transfer between hosts (a task, an image,
a workflow image) holds one source client and one destination client for the
whole operation. The native host registry, SSH tunnels, and Keychain tokens
stay in `lib/daemons.ts` and `lib/desktop.ts`.

### API types

`ui/src/lib/api-types.generated.ts` holds the TypeScript types of every
response that `/api/openapi.json` describes. `npm run api-types` in `ui/`
generates it from the committed snapshot
`internal/commands/testdata/openapi.json`, and the `ui-api-types` step of
`make frontend-check` fails when the file is out of date. Do not edit it; see
[Go control plane and plugins](/docs/development#go-control-plane-and-plugins)
for the workflow after an API change.

Each schema is a top-level type with the Go type's name, such as `AgentRow`
or `TaskDetail`. A domain module re-exports the types that its callers need,
for example `export type { AgentRow, AgentView } from "../api-types.generated"`,
and components import them from `@/lib/api`. `Comment` and `Event` would
shadow DOM globals, so `tasks.ts` re-exports them as `TaskComment` and
`TaskEvent`. Where the spec has a plain
string and the UI needs a union, the module narrows it at one place, such as
`taskPriority(task)`.

The types follow the spec exactly. A list that Go can return as `null` is
`T[] | null`, and an optional field is optional, so the code handles both.
Test data is a complete response, not a partial literal; the factories in
`ui/src/test/fixtures/apiFixtures.ts` fill the fields a test does not check.

These types stay hand-written. Each response type among them has a comment
that says why the spec does not cover it:

- Responses that `internal/api/server.go` serves outside the command
  registry: the agent event stream (`AgentEvent`), the tasks WebSocket frame
  (`TaskEventHint`), the mail WebSocket frame (`MailHint`), and the image, team, and workflow image archive imports.
- The transcript calls of `audit.ts`, which the spec describes only as
  objects.
- Request bodies and filters, such as `CreateAgentSpec` and `TaskFilters`, and
  types that the UI derives, such as `AgentPromptLayer`.

## Code splitting

The first download contains only the shell: the titlebar, the agent list, the
providers, server selection, and the agent workspace frame. Everything else
loads with `React.lazy` when it first renders:

- the server pages in `TerminalsRoutes` (Tasks, All tasks, Activity, Images,
  Workflows, Stores, and Settings) and the nested image and settings routes of
  `routes.tsx`;
- every agent workspace tab and the Goal task drawer in `AgentWorkspace`;
- the TipTap editor (`tasks/TaskMarkdownEditor.tsx`): `MarkdownEditor` in
  `TaskMarkdown.tsx` is a lazy wrapper, so `MarkdownContent` never loads TipTap;
- the file viewer of `FileBrowser`, with CodeMirror, its languages, and the
  highlighted preview.

`components/LazyBoundary` wraps each place that renders a lazy component. It
sits inside the layout that stays mounted, so the titlebar, the agent list,
and the server or settings navigation stay visible. While a chunk downloads,
the content area shows a `role="status"` text, **Loading…**. A later open uses
the loaded module. A navigation inside the router is a transition, so the
previous screen stays until the next one is ready. If a chunk fails to load,
for example after an update or when the server is unreachable, the boundary
shows **This screen failed to load.** and **Reloading discards unsaved input.**
with a **Reload** button. It never retries by itself. A new route path, tab,
or file clears the error.

`vite.desktop.config.ts` puts vendor libraries in named chunks with
`build.rolldownOptions.output.codeSplitting.groups`, the Vite 8 replacement for
`manualChunks`: `react` (React, React DOM, and the router), `codemirror`,
`tiptap` (TipTap and ProseMirror), `xterm`, and `markdown` (react-markdown,
remark, rehype, and highlight.js). One more group, `api`, holds the app's own
HTTP client (`src/lib/api/`, `lib/daemons.ts`, and `lib/storage.ts`): the shell
and most lazy screens share it, and without the group the bundler folds it into
the entry chunk once enough screens share it. Only `react` and `api` are part of
the first download; each other group loads with the first screen that needs it. Keep a group
narrow: if the shell imports one module of a group, the whole group becomes
part of the first download.

`npm run bundle:budget`, a step of `make frontend-check`, has three limits in
bytes before compression. The entry chunk is limited to 351,000 bytes. The
entry chunk plus its static imports is limited to 723,000 bytes. All JavaScript
chunks, lazily loaded ones included, are limited to 3,215,000 bytes. The step
fails when a size is over its limit. The budget does not measure CSS or the
start time on a device.

## Component boundaries

The public screen components keep their existing imports and properties.
Their internal modules separate form state, requests, and presentation:

- `terminals/create-agent` owns the single creation draft, source and image
  loading, request validation, and the Target, Identity, Runtime, Loop, and
  Lifecycle sections. Submission keeps creation separate from a retry of Start.
- `terminals/server-dialog` separates HTTPS and SSH forms from host-operation
  events and progress. The operation result remains separate from connectivity.
- `components/file-browser` separates the tree, toolbar, viewer, dialogs, and
  file actions. `FileBrowser` keeps the public API and source reset boundary.
- `agents/configuration` owns the configuration blocks. The existing draft and
  commit modules still own the single Save operation for the page.
- `mailbox` is one two-pane mailbox for both Mailbox tabs: `Mailbox` holds
  the box switch and the panes, `MailboxList`, `MailboxLetter` and
  `MailboxCompose` render them, `mailboxModel` holds the pure readings, and
  `mailQueries` the query keys and the live refetch.
- Tasks separates local view state, panel sizing, query composition, and write
  actions. `TaskDetail` keeps one draft with its original revision. Its fields,
  relations, history, and dialogs render that state without another server cache.
- `components/tui-screen` separates the xterm lifecycle and sizing hook and the
  tmux scrollback hook from the toolbar, compose, and help markup. The input
  handler stays stable, so a render does not recreate the terminal.
- `lib/audit.ts` and `lib/auditCodex.ts` read an audit record through handler
  tables keyed by event kind, harness message type, and Codex item type.
  `components/audit` renders each row kind in its own small component and keeps
  the full log's filter and paging state in hooks.
- `pages/audit-log` separates the URL query and the polled iteration list from
  the list and tag editor markup.

## Shared helpers and styles

Helpers that more than one screen needs live in `ui/src/lib/`, and each name
is declared once:

- `lib/errors.ts` exports `errorText(error)`. It returns the message of any
  `Error`, `ApiError` included, and `String(error)` for other values. A plain
  error therefore shows `Failed to fetch`, without the class name.
- `lib/ids.ts` exports `idempotencyKey(prefix)`. It returns
  `crypto.randomUUID()`, or `prefix-<time>-<random>` when the WebView has no
  `randomUUID`.
- `lib/statusTone.ts` exports `flexibleStatusLabel(status)` for a flexible
  task status. `lib/tasks.ts` alone exports `taskStatusLabel(task)`, the label
  of any task.

Styles are Tailwind utilities on the element. The `@theme` block of
`ui/src/index.css` names the dense text sizes and the radii between the
`--radius` steps:

| Utility | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `text-nano`, `text-micro`, `text-tiny`, `text-caption`, `text-meta` | 9, 10, 10.5, 11, 11.5 px |
| `text-ui`, `text-body-sm`, `text-body`, `text-body-lg`, `text-title` | 12, 12.5, 13, 14, 15 px |
| `rounded-hair`, `rounded-xs`, `rounded-chip`, `rounded-sm`, `rounded-control` | 1.5, 2, 5, 6, 7 px |
| `rounded-md`, `rounded-panel`, `rounded-lg`, `rounded-card`, `rounded-xl` | 8, 9, 10, 12, 14 px |

The text sizes set only `font-size`, so the element keeps its line height.
Sizes, spacing, and ring widths use the 4 px spacing scale: `h-6.5` is 26 px.
`cn()` in `lib/utils.ts` tells tailwind-merge about the new names. Without
that, tailwind-merge reads `text-ui` as a color and drops the color class next
to it. When you add a text size or a radius to `@theme`, add it to `cn()` too.
`ui/src/lib/utils.test.ts` fails when the two lists differ.

`ui/src/test/arbitraryPxPolicy.test.ts` fails when production code under
`ui/src` or `ui/store` uses a class of the form `utility-[Npx]`. Composite
values, such as `grid-cols-[76px_minmax(0,1fr)]`, are allowed. The shadcn
primitives under `ui/src/components/ui/` are not checked, so they stay the same
as upstream. An inline `style` is only for a value that the code calculates at
run time, such as a column width or a CSS variable.

A CSS file is only for a rule that utilities cannot express clearly:
pseudo-elements, a media query for one widget, or a rule that must override
another component. `ui/src/pages/tasks/tasks.css` lists the rules it keeps
and gives the reason for each at its top.

## WebView storage

`ui/src/lib/storage.ts` owns all access to `localStorage` and `sessionStorage`
in the Desktop UI and the Store UI. It declares every key in one registry with
its area, name, version, parser, and fallback value. Other modules call
`readKey`, `writeKey`, and `removeKey` with a key from that registry. The unit
test `ui/src/test/webStoragePolicy.test.ts` fails when production code under
`ui/src` or `ui/store` uses `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, or
`window.dispatchEvent` directly. It scans the sources because the lint policy
allows no per-file oxlint overrides. Tests and fixtures still seed raw values,
so they detect a change of a stored format.

Storage access is best effort. A missing value, a value the parser rejects,
broken JSON, and storage that throws (blocked, private mode) all read as the
fallback value. A failed write returns `false` and does not throw, so the
interface keeps its state in memory until a reload. A read that finds a bad
value does not delete it; the next write replaces it. Values are never logged,
because some of them are tokens.

Key names did not change when the registry was added, so saved state survives
upgrades. A new key uses the form `<area>:<purpose>:v<N>`, and the registry
test requires a versioned name to end with its version. When a format changes
incompatibly, the key gets a new name with the next version. The old name
stays in the registry only so it can be read once, like `terminals:workspace:v1`.

| Key | Area | Owner | Value | Fallback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tariboy-theme` | local | theme provider | `light`, `dark`, or `system` | `system` |
| `app:ui-mode:v1` | local | interface mode | `simple` or `expert` | `simple` |
| `app:workspaces:v1` | local | host workspaces | JSON workspaces, host map, active workspace | Default only |
| `desktop:updates:auto-download:v1` | local | Desktop updates | `true` or `false` | `true` |
| `tariboy:runtime-presets:v1` | local | create-agent presets | JSON saved models and efforts per harness | none |
| `tariboy_daemons` | local | browser host registry | JSON host metadata list | empty |
| `tariboy_active_daemon` | local | host registry | selected host ID | none |
| `tariboy_daemons_rejected_cleartext` | local | Desktop host migration | JSON cleartext hosts not imported | none |
| `tariboy_daemon_token_<id>` | session | browser host registry | host token (browser mode only; Desktop uses the Keychain) | empty |
| `tariboy:team-import` | local | Groups | JSON pending team import ID and host | none |
| `terminals:server-order:v1` | local | sidebar | JSON host order | registry order |
| `terminals:sidebar:v1` | local | sidebar | JSON width and hidden state | 268px, shown |
| `terminals:workspace:v1` | local | sidebar (legacy, read once) | JSON record of the removed canvas | none |
| `terminals:sidebar-tab:v1` | local | sidebar | `servers` or `agents` | `servers` |
| `terminals:sidebar-pinned:v1` | local | sidebar | JSON pinned agents | none |
| `tui:draft:<agent>:<section>` | local | inject modal | draft text | empty |
| `tasks:columns:v1` | local | task tables | JSON column order and widths | default layout |
| `tasks:workspace:v1` | local | task detail panel | JSON detail width | half the window |
| `tasks:new-task-queue:v1` | local | new task form | JSON last queue per server | none |
| `tasks:queue-filter:v1` | session | task queue filter | queue prefix | none |
| `tasks:all-view:v1` | session | All tasks | JSON search, status view, and server | active, all servers |
| `tariboy_store_token` | session | Store UI | Store bearer token | none |

### Image change notifications

`ui/src/lib/imageEvents.ts` connects image builds to the image lists in the
same window. A finished build from a directory or from a Store calls
`notifyImagesChanged()`. **Built images** and the agent configuration sources
subscribe with `subscribeImagesChanged()` and reload the images of their
current host. A failing subscriber does not stop the others. Builds outside
this window, for example from the CLI, do not notify the lists.

## Server data in Tasks

TanStack Query v5 owns the server data for Tasks. One QueryClient serves the
application, and each component test uses an isolated client. The migrated
read owners are TasksWorkspace, TaskDrawer, and WorkflowPanel. TaskDetail
keeps form drafts and uses a mutation for relation writes.

A query key identifies one response. Its prefix is
the server identity, followed by the Tasks resource and its parameters.
List keys include the agent scope, text, status view, assignee, and waiting
principal. Queue filtering remains local. History keys distinguish the
workspace's latest 200 events from the drawer's first 200 events.

Queries read the server from the surrounding `ApiProvider`; a client for
the local daemon has the identity `local`. Server identity is independent of its endpoint. A new SSH port cancels old
reads and refreshes active queries without changing their keys or form state.
An unavailable endpoint disables background reads. Credentials never appear
in query keys, logs, or persistent storage. Credential changes clear that
server's old data, and removing a host removes its cached queries.

The cache holds data only in memory. Inactive queries expire after five
minutes. Data is stale immediately, so reopening a view refreshes it in the
background. Automatic retries, window-focus refresh, and browser reconnect
refresh are disabled. The host connection adapter controls reconnect reads.
When the page becomes visible again or the browser comes back online, the
client rereads all active queries once (see [API layer](#api-layer)).
Network failures retain a loaded snapshot. A 401 or 403 response clears the
server's cached data and shows the access error.

HTTP responses remain authoritative. The task socket opens after HTTP supplies
its starting sequence. The event adapter combines a burst into one refresh
cycle per server and query client, including one notification read. Multiple
subscribers deduplicate the same event sequence. An event during a cycle requests a
trailing cycle. Socket frames never replace task records.

Writes cancel competing reads before and after the operation. They then
invalidate the same server's task queries, so lists, details, history,
notifications, and workflows refresh together. An optimistic tree move restores
the previous rows on failure and reads the server again. A rejected save keeps
its draft, including after a revision conflict. Writes do not retry or queue
for an offline host. WorkflowPanel owns workflow-action refreshes; its parent
does not start a second cycle. A successful notification-read write cancels
intervening inbox reads before updating the read marker. It marks the inbox
stale for the next socket, manual, or mount refresh.

For another Tasks reader, reuse its typed query options:

~~~tsx
const api = useApi()
const detail = useApiQuery(taskQueries.detail(api, taskKey))
~~~

Keep selection, drafts, expansion, sizing, and focus in the component.
Pass the query's AbortSignal through every paginated read. The shared layer
discards cancelled results. New resources need keys for every response parameter.

Terminals, the aggregate task list, the attention coordinator, and
standalone queue forms retain their existing loaders. Their migration belongs
to separate work. The drawer opened from those screens already shares the
Tasks queries. Specialized workflow actions and log readers retain their own
state.

Tasks uses one reusable workspace at `/servers/:hostId/tasks` and inside each
Agent tab. The server route shows every task visible on that host;
an Agent tab sends
`scope_agent=<name>` to render only that agent's inherited view. The tree fills
the full width of the island and is expandable, ordered at every
depth by priority, manual position, and
task key, with inline creation and same-queue drag reparenting. Before/after
drag reordering stays within the task's P0-P3 priority bucket, while dropping
inside a task reparents it without changing priority. Compact priority markers
appear in the tree; on a task the viewer can edit, clicking the marker opens a
P0-P3 menu that saves only the new priority with the row's revision, without
opening the task. A revision conflict reloads the tree and shows the error.
Read-only (`context` or `respond`) tasks keep a plain marker. A click anywhere on
a row selects its task, except on the row's own controls: the priority marker and
its menu, the expand chevron, the drag grip, and the add-child button. From the
keyboard, the title button selects the task. Selecting a task opens its detail in a right-side sheet over
the still-mounted tree, with priority, other task fields, comments, mentions,
and answer waits. The sheet starts at half the viewport width. Its keyboard- and
pointer-accessible left separator resizes it, and the pixel width persists in
`tasks:workspace:v1`. Back, Close, Escape, or a backdrop click dismisses the
sheet while preserving the tree's expansion and scroll position. Dismissal
protects unsaved task, comment, and relation drafts with the confirmation
“Are you sure you want to close this task? Unsaved changes will be discarded.”
Task Detail also offers `Wait customer` status and an editable `Pull request`
field; both use the existing optimistic revision and explicit-host request path.
The sheet is one `--card` island with its own scroll and a sticky identity
header carrying the task key, title, status and assignee. A single banner under
that header reports what needs a person — an unanswered customer question — and
other statuses speak through the status pill alone. The sheet opens as soon as a task is
chosen, in Tasks or from a letter, showing the task key and a loading line until
the task and its history arrive; refreshing the task already open keeps the
loaded panel in place. History rows read as time, kind, a
one-line `key value · key value` payload summary and actor; the panel never
prints a raw JSON payload.
The sheet is a modal `Dialog` at `z-[60]`, so every floating primitive that can
open from inside it — dropdown menu, select, context menu, tooltip, and the
alert dialog that confirms an action — stacks at `z-[70]`; at the old `z-50`
they opened under the sheet's overlay and took no click.
The detail sheet's own keyboard- and pointer-accessible separator is the only
one the workspace has. Arrow keys move it, Shift increases the step, Home and
double-click restore its default, and the clamped width persists in the
versioned WebView localStorage record `tasks:workspace:v1`. Route changes and
app reloads restore that record; a record written before the task rail was
removed still reads, its rail width ignored. A task opened from a letter uses
the same sheet, separator, and stored width, clamped to the window instead of
the workspace, so a resize in either place carries over to the other.

A task with a workflow (`workflow_digest` set, or `workflow_name` as a
fallback, tested by `isWorkflowTask`) is presented by category; the daemon's
`status_view` (Active, Closed, All) selects by category too, and a flexible
task's category equals its status. `TaskRow` takes its tone from `task.category` and its
label from `taskStatusLabel(task)`: the workflow status ID, humanised, in a
clipped pill whose title is the ID, then the task's `workflow_step` as `k/n`
(hidden on a phone), plus a `waiting_on` marker (`customer`, `script`, or a
danger `paused` whose title is the pause reason). A `workflow_attention` of
kind `failed`, `script_failed`, or `rejected` replaces the `customer`/`script`
marker with a problem mark whose title is the message; the pause pill
outranks it, and `idle` earns no mark. The row needs no request of its own:
both objects come with the task JSON. `TaskDetail`
compares `status` only with `category` for its dirty check and tone, and sends
no `status` or `assignee` on Save for a workflow task. Its assignee is
`WorkflowAssignee`: in an open, unpaused pool status of the shared workflow
query it is a select of that pool's members (`listAgentPools` through
`taskQueries.pools`) that calls `reassignTaskWorkflow` on change and then
`onTaskChanged`; otherwise it is text. `TaskDetail` hides **Move to
another server…** for one, and neither its banner nor a comment chip asks for
a comment on the workflow's own (`system:workflow`) wait. In place of the status
select it renders `WorkflowPanel`, which reads the shared workflow query. A task revision, an event sequence, or
a completed write marks that query stale, so a workflow event refreshes the
panel even when the task revision stays the same. It composes, top down,
`WorkflowPauseBanner` (`resumeTaskWorkflow`, `cancelWorkflowTask`),
`WorkflowProblem` (the one problem `explainProblem` in `explainWorkflowProblem.ts`
picks from the view, with `retryTransitionRequest` behind **Retry** and the
run's log through `RunRow` with `autoLoad`), `WorkflowStepper` (the view's
`statuses` as steps, marked by `stepMarks` in `workflowGraph.ts`; the panel
owns the selected step, which starts at the current status and follows it
until the customer picks a step), the header with `stepOf`,
`WorkflowOutcomes` (`advanceTask`), `WorkflowArtifacts`
(`setTaskArtifact`, `getTaskArtifactHistory`; for the selected step only the
artifacts `stepArtifacts` finds in the `requires` of a transition into it,
then out of it, each naming its transition; **Show all artifacts**, or a
second click on the step, clears the selection and lists every entry of the
view's `declared_artifacts` in one list, those `requiredBy` names for the
current status first), `WorkflowRuns`
(`getTaskScriptRunLog`; `runTone` gives each row its tone), the visit list,
and the header's labeled **Run watch now**, **Return to agent…**, **Upgrade to
NAME@VERSION…**, **Move to status…**, and **Cancel task** buttons: **Run watch
now** appears when `canRunWatch` finds an open, unpaused script status with a
watch, is disabled while `hasActiveRun` finds a pending or running run, and
sends `runTaskWatch`, then refetches the view; `ReturnToAgent` picks its
targets with `returnTargets` and sends `advanceTask` or `moveTaskWorkflow`, the
upgrade form appears when `canUpgrade` finds the view's `queue_digest` differs
from its `digest` and sends `upgradeTaskWorkflow`, the move form uses
`moveTaskWorkflow` (targets from the view's `statuses`), and cancel uses
`cancelWorkflowTask`. The move and upgrade forms live in
`WorkflowMoveForms.tsx`. `stepMarks`, `returnTargets`, and `defaultReturnTarget`
read `runVisits`, the visits of the task's current workflow digest. Outcomes, the problem block, and the return form follow
a transition request through `useFollowRequest` in `workflowShared.ts`
(`getTransitionRequest` once a second until the request settles or
`wait_seconds` passes). Destructive actions confirm through
the controlled alert dialog of `useWorkflowConfirm`; `workflowShared.ts` also holds
`errorText` and `useMounted`. Messages and logs render as React text;
artifact values render through `MarkdownContent`, or as React text when an
artifact is switched to **Text**. Every call uses the client of the surrounding
`ApiProvider`. After a drawer action `TasksWorkspace` reloads the tree as well as
the detail, so the row agrees with the drawer before the socket reports the
change. Queue settings are `QueueSettingsDialog`: a large `Dialog` (full
screen on a phone) with the queue list on the left and the selected queue in
tabs on the right. `QueueSettingsDetail.tsx` renders the selected queue and
the new-queue form; `queueSettingsModel.ts` holds the pure readings: a list
row's summary and warning, the tabs, the form requests, and how a refused bind
reads. When it opens it reads each queue's binding
(`getQueueWorkflow`), the bound manifest (`getWorkflowImage` by digest), and
its pools (`listAgentPools`), so each list row can show the workflow and a dot
for a required pool without agents; a queue that fails to load shows an error
with **Retry** instead of a guess. `listTaskPrincipals` supplies the agent
suggestions. The dialog keeps the pools as the one source the tabs share. The
**Workflow** tab, `QueueWorkflowSettings` (`getQueueWorkflow`,
`setQueueWorkflow`, `clearQueueWorkflow`, `listWorkflowImages`,
`getWorkflowImage`), shows the binding, with the tag it follows when it has
one, and `WorkflowStatusMap`: the statuses of
the bound image, or of the image chosen in the select before **Bind**, with
their owners and outcomes; a pool chip opens the **Pools** tab. A refused bind
lists the empty pools, which shrink as pools gain agents, or the missing
secrets, each with a button to its tab (**Open Environment** for secrets). The **Pools** tab, `QueuePools`
(`rebindAgentPool`), lists the required pools, the pools a refused bind named,
and the queue's pools as rows of
agent chips and saves a row's full list with its revision; a
`revision_conflict` reloads the queue. The Workflow and Pools tabs stay mounted
while hidden, so a refusal and unsaved pool edits survive a tab switch; closing
the dialog drops them. The **Environment** tab, `QueueEnvironment`, holds two blocks. **Env**
(`listQueueEnv`, `setQueueEnv`, `removeQueueEnv`) lists plain env vars with
their values. **Secrets**, `QueueSecrets` (`listQueueSecrets`,
`setQueueSecret`, `removeQueueSecret`), lists keys only: the value lives in a
password input until it is sent and is never read back. A key is one kind or
the other, so setting a key of the other block asks first, and a change in
either block reloads both. A name a refused bind reported counts as set by
either block. For a bound queue, the dialog passes the loaded definition, and
`workflowEnvHints` reads its `env` keys and `requires_secrets` as suggested
names. Both blocks set a key through `KeyValueForm`: its key input gets a
`<datalist>` of them, and a chip shows for each name neither block holds. A chip fills the
key and focuses the value; an **Env** chip shows the Workflowfile default on
hover. The **Sources** tab of a
bound queue, `QueueSources` (`listQueueSources`, `getQueueSourceRunLog`) lists the sources of
the workflow with their schedule, failures in a row, and newest 20 runs; it
loads once and on **Reload**, without polling. Its run rows and the task's
`WorkflowRuns` share `RunRow`, which reads a log only on **Log**, renders it as
text, and offers **Refresh** while the run is going. A flexible task renders
exactly as before. The browser suite covers the path against an isolated daemon.

One toolbar sits above the table in both places. It carries the search field,
the `Active | Closed | All` segment, the queue control, the `My tasks` and
`Waiting for me` chips — off by default, and still the daemon's `assignee` and
`waiting_for` filters — the agent chip in an Agent tab, refresh, and
**New task**. The queue control opens a menu of `All queues` and every queue
with the number of tasks it contributes to the current list, and
`Manage queues…` under a separator opens the queue settings dialog: the queue
list with **New queue**, and the selected queue in **General** (the existing
`PATCH`), **Workflow**, **Pools**, **Environment**, and, for a bound queue,
**Sources** tabs. The queue
filter is applied in the client so that menu can count from the load the tree
already performs; `scope_agent`, `status_view`, the text search, `assignee` and
`waiting_for` stay daemon-side. The **New task** form preselects the queue
selected in the filter. When `All queues` is selected, it preselects the queue
of the last root task created from a form on that server, or the first queue
when that queue no longer exists. After a root task is created, its queue is
saved in `localStorage` under `tasks:new-task-queue:v1`, a JSON object from
server (`local` for the local daemon, otherwise the Desktop server id) to queue
prefix. A child task, a cancelled form, or a failed create saves nothing. The
record survives a restart, stays on one device, and is ignored when it is
unreadable.

The table header and its rows read one column layout, so a column cannot
drift from its heading. By default `Pri` comes first in every table, then
`Key`, 168px holding the tree indents, the chevron and the key, which truncates
rather than wrapping; `Task` takes the rest. The agent table adds `Duration` — the task's first move to
`in_progress` (`started_at`) to completion, or to now while the task is open,
and `—` for a task never started — and the server table adds `Agent`. There is no
`Queue` column: the key prefix already names the queue. In the server table the
header is sticky. The drag grip lives in the row's left padding and appears on
hover.

The column order and widths are the user's. One order covers the agent, server
and every-server tables; each shows its own columns in that order. Every column
except `Task` has its own width, from 40px to 480px (`Key` from 96px, `Pri`
from 24px); `Task` can move but always takes the rest of the row, so very wide
columns on a narrow screen squeeze it. The layout is the versioned WebView
localStorage record `tasks:columns:v1`, written on every change and read once
per page load, so it survives a reload or an app restart on that device; it is
not synced between devices. An unreadable record, an unknown column or an
out-of-range width falls back to the default for that part, and when storage
is unavailable changes last until the next reload.

- **Width:** the edge after each header cell is a `separator`. A mouse or a
  finger drags it (Pointer Events with capture, `touch-action: none`, a 16px
  target on a coarse pointer); arrows step 8px, Shift+arrows 32px, and Home or
  a double click restores the default.
- **Order:** a header label is a drag grip in its own drag context, apart from
  the row drags. A mouse starts after 5px, a finger after a 250ms press, so a
  swipe still scrolls; Space or Enter starts a keyboard move.
- **Columns menu:** the `Columns` button in the filter bar lists the current
  table's columns with one-tap `Narrow`/`Widen` (16px) and left/right moves,
  and `Reset columns`. It is the touch path on a phone or tablet and stays
  open between steps.

Task descriptions and comments use the MIT-licensed Tiptap OSS visual editor
with an explicit Markdown source mode. Headings, bold, italic, strikethrough,
links, lists, checklists, code, and tables are supported. Unsupported blocks
remain visible and editable as literal code blocks in rich mode; the
Markdown source stays available as an explicit manual mode. A `Rich text |
Markdown` segment selects the mode, and in Task Detail it sits on the section's
own label row beside `Send files` rather than inside the editor.
Empty numbered-list items remain editable in rich text, including immediately
after Enter adds a new item; they do not add an extra visible paragraph.
Blank lines typed at the end of the text stay in the rich editor for further
typing but are left out of the emitted Markdown, because a trailing empty
paragraph has no Markdown form and would otherwise be written as an `&nbsp;`
entity and shown back as a literal code block.
The comment form appears before newest-first comments and after oldest-first comments.
Saved content renders through `react-markdown` and `remark-gfm`, without raw
HTML execution. Markdown strings remain the API and persistence contract;
editor documents are not stored. Each saved comment exposes a copy action on
hover or keyboard focus that writes its original Markdown string to the
clipboard. Long text and links wrap within the task
panel, while wide tables and code blocks scroll inside their own Markdown
block. In Desktop, absolute `http://` and `https://` links in descriptions and
comments open through the native system-browser command instead of navigating
the WebView; relative links and ordinary browser builds keep normal anchor
behavior. Vite's `build.license` generates bundled
JavaScript dependency license texts and copyright notices in
`desktop/dist/THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES.md` on each Desktop build; this generated
asset is packaged with the app and is not committed.
The comment form defaults its Ask selector to the task assignee, while typed
mentions, explicit questions, and answer-wait semantics remain daemon-owned.
Beside **Send comment**, a secondary **Send Ok** action includes the selected
Ask mention and posts `Ok` without changing the Ask selection. It is hidden
as soon as the comment contains text.

### Mailbox

Mail is the only messaging surface. There are two **Mailbox** tabs, and both
render one component, `pages/mailbox/Mailbox.tsx`. It shows one principal's
mailbox: a segmented **Inbox** / **Sent** / **Archive** switch, where Inbox
carries the open letter count from `GET /api/mail/unread`, and **Compose**.
The list is on the left and the selected letter on the right. Below the
`DRAWER_QUERY` breakpoint only one pane shows: the list, or the letter with a
**Back** button. A row shows the sender (the recipient in Sent), the subject
with tags for a kind other than `message`, a notice, and a dead letter
(`dead · <reason>`), a one-line preview, the time, and a dot while the letter is
unread. The letter shows From, To, Received and its state (open, answered,
archived with its note, dead), a line naming the letter it replies to (read
with `mail.show`), and the body as Markdown through the task pipeline, with no
raw HTML. Sent and Archive load more pages with **Load more**.

Opening an unread Inbox letter marks it read. The daemon closes a read notice,
so it moves to Archive and stays open in the right pane; a request stays in the
Inbox until **Reply** or **Archive**. A letter with a string `data.task_key`
shows **Open** with the task key, which opens the task drawer (`TaskDrawer`) over the
mailbox: the route does not change, the letter stays selected, and closing the
drawer returns to it. A `task.question` letter is answered on its task: it
shows **Answer on the task**, which opens that drawer, and no **Reply**.
**Compose** opens a dialog
with the recipient, the subject, the text and a **No reply needed** switch: off
sends a request, on sends a notice. Every write shows a toast with the daemon's
message on failure and refetches; nothing changes optimistically. The lists
refetch on every `/api/mail/ws` hint for the mailbox's principal (every hint for
the customer) and on every reconnect, through `useMailSocket` in
`hooks/useMailSocket.ts`.

**Server → Mailbox** (`/servers/<host>/mail`) is the first server section,
before Tasks. It is the customer's mailbox: no `as` is sent, so the daemon acts
as the customer. The recipient picker lists the host's agents. The section
label carries the customer's open letter count, kept live by the mail socket.

**Agent → Mailbox** is the first agent tab, in Simple and Expert mode. It is
that agent's mailbox, read with `as=agent:<name>`, so the operator replies on
the agent's behalf. **Compose** writes from the customer to that agent; the
recipient is fixed. The toolbar shows `batch N · inbox K/M`: N is the agent's
`messages_batch` (letters per iteration), K its open inbox (`messages_pending`)
and M its cap (`messages_max_queue`). A letter over the cap is dead on arrival
and shows in Archive with its tag and **Requeue**. **Clear inbox** opens a
destructive confirmation; confirming posts `/api/agents/<name>/mail/clear`,
which deletes the agent's open letters, and reports how many. The tab carries
the open inbox count as a badge, and the header shows **Inbox full: K / M**
when the inbox is at its cap. Configuration names the two fields
**Mail: letters per iteration** and **Mail: maximum open inbox**.

The sidebar mounts one `/api/mail/ws` socket per server. Its frames are
refetch hints, never authority: a hint reloads the typed HTTP response, and a
reconnect reloads unconditionally because the socket replays nothing. A frame
names the letter: `{id, from, to, kind, ts}`. The sidebar refetches its agents
on a hint, so it changes as a letter lands rather than on the next poll.

Beside it, the sidebar mounts one `/api/agent-states/ws` socket per host. Its
frames `{agent, type, ts}` say that an iteration event or a state change
(start, stop, status line, halt, idle stop) happened for
that agent. The sidebar refetches its agents at most once a second
on these hints, and the agent header refetches its status on a hint for its own
agent. While every host's state socket is open, the sidebar polls every 15
seconds and the agent header every 15 seconds as a fallback. A host without the
socket (an older daemon) keeps the 3-second polls. The daemon banner probes
`/api/daemon/status` every 10 seconds.

An agent's **Scripts** view exposes **Exec** for any completed definition —
including a recurring one that stopped after publishing its result — and for an
active recurring definition with no pending or running attempt. Exec queues the
stored command through the ordinary script worker; a recurring definition
resumes its fixed post-completion delay from there while its runs stay quiet.

The Tasks workspace has no inbox of its own: the questions are letters, and
the workspace renders them as one indicator. It reads the customer's Inbox
(`GET /api/mail?box=inbox`) and keeps the `task.question` letters. A small red
indicator on a task row identifies an unread question for that task, and
opening that task marks those letters read, which is the only thing that clears
the indicator in the UI. The unfiltered **Active** view, without a search, also
lists a closed task that still has such an unread question (in an agent's
workspace, one asked by that agent), read by its key, so the question can be
opened and cleared; it leaves the view once read.

A route-independent coordinator watches every configured host. Its source is
`GET /api/mail/unread` for the customer: the open letters counted by sender and
kind. The `task.question` rows from an `agent:` sender make the shared
attention, which orders the agent list and puts a count on the agent
workspace's **Tasks** tab: the number of open questions from that agent, the
questions waiting for the customer's answer. Reading a question does not lower
it; the answer recorded on the task closes the letter, and the count drops.
Customer-authored questions contribute to neither.

Each host watcher treats typed HTTP task and mail responses as
authoritative. The resumable task WebSocket and the mail WebSocket (a
`task.question` hint) supply refresh hints, and the task socket sequence
progress; a hint triggers an HTTP refetch and never mutates attention by
itself. The counts carry no letter ids, so the watcher also reads the
customer's Inbox for the baseline, and again only when an agent's question
count rises. Initial host discovery and recovery both establish a silent
baseline: current questions populate the in-app indicators, but do not replay
native notifications. Observed letter IDs and per-host snapshots exist only in
React memory for the current Desktop session. They are not written to Web
Storage or persisted by the daemon, and current-session ID tracking deduplicates
repeated hints and snapshots.

For a newly observed unread agent question after the baseline, the
coordinator asks the native bridge to show one notification with only
`host_id`, `notification_id` (the letter id), and `task_key` in its activation
payload. Native permission
denial, unsupported notification delivery, and send failures are fallbacks:
they do not alter the authoritative HTTP snapshot or remove in-app attention.
Activation uses the original explicit host, marks the exact letter read,
refreshes that host, and navigates to
`/servers/:hostId/tasks?task=<key>` (the packaged hash route is
`#/servers/:hostId/tasks?task=<key>`), where the task detail is selected. A
failed read does not block that navigation, and an unresolved remote host is
never replaced with local authority.

Task changes arrive over the resumable `/api/tasks/ws?after=<sequence>` socket.
Hints trigger typed HTTP refetches; they never replace authoritative task
responses. A surface opens the socket only once it knows the host's current
sequence, read from the authoritative HTTP snapshot it already loads, so it
never asks the daemon to replay the whole task log. Remote targets map HTTP(S) to WS(S) and put the existing bearer
token in the WebSocket query because browser sockets cannot set an
Authorization header.

Queue settings expose explicit pool membership, edited with the revisioned
pool route, the workflow binding with the statuses of the image, and queue
secrets. The UI does not edit a workflow definition, and it does not infer
phases from title prefixes or assignee. Operator history remains available after completion. See
[Task workflows](/docs/task-workflows).

The navigation hierarchy is **Server → Agent**.
A selected server owns Mailbox, Tasks, Activity, Images, Workflow images, Stores, and Settings, and its
context row remains visible above the selected agent's Mailbox, Tasks, Terminal,
Activity, Configuration, and Advanced tabs. There is no Autopilot tab: an old
`/autopilot` route is treated as an unknown tab. Server-owned routes include
the explicit host id and fail closed rather than silently falling back to local.

### Host workspaces

A workspace is a named group of registered hosts in one app window. The
titlebar shows the current workspace right after the sidebar toggle; its menu
lists every workspace with its host count and a check on the current one,
followed by **New workspace…** and **Manage workspaces…**. Choosing a workspace
narrows the agent sidebar, its Servers tab and its `N servers · M agents` footer
to that workspace's hosts. When the open agent's host is not in it, its first
agent opens in the same tab, or the island shows `<name> has no agents yet`
with a **Manage workspaces** button when it has none. Polling continues for
every host, so the manager can show each host as ready or offline, and agents
on hosts outside the current workspace keep running: a workspace filters the
window, it does not isolate hosts.

**Default** is built in and cannot be renamed or deleted, and every host
belongs to exactly one workspace. A host without an assignment, including a
newly added one, is in Default. The manager dialog creates a workspace (Enter or
**Create workspace**; blank names are ignored) and selects it, renames a custom
workspace as its name is typed without ever saving a blank one, and moves a
host with **Move to…** and a click on the target workspace. **Delete
workspace** asks inline and returns the workspace's hosts to Default; deleting
the current workspace switches to Default.

The state is the WebView localStorage record `app:workspaces:v1`:
`{version: 1, workspaces: [{id, name}], hostWorkspace: {hostId: workspaceId},
active}`. It is local to one app installation and is not stored by any daemon,
because hosts are the set of daemons rather than something one daemon owns.
Malformed storage, unavailable storage, or an assignment to a missing workspace
falls back to Default.

### All tasks

The titlebar carries an `Agents | All tasks` segment, next to the sidebar
toggle in **Agents**. The view is the `view=all` query on the current route, so it survives
a reload, Back returns to the previous view, and the selected agent's path is
untouched. Arrow keys move between the two options. In **All tasks** the
agent sidebar and its titlebar toggle are hidden, and the island shows one task
table for every server instead of the agent's header and tabs. The persisted
sidebar visibility is not changed, so switching back to **Agents** restores the
sidebar as it was and reopens the agent the route still names.

The table reads `GET /api/tasks` from the local daemon and every registered
server in parallel, each with its own token, following each server's cursor to
the end; a server's live `/api/tasks/ws` hint re-reads only that server. A
server that the sidebar cannot reach, or whose read fails, keeps the other
servers' rows and adds a `<server> unavailable · Retry` line above the table.
Rows are keyed by server and task key, because a transferred task keeps its key
and leaves a cancelled copy behind. Trees are built within each server; roots
are ordered newest-updated first. Six skeleton rows show until the first
server answers.

Columns are Pri, Key, Task, Agent, Server, Status and Updated. There is no drag
reparenting or inline child creation, since neither crosses servers. A priority
picked on a row is saved on that row's server, which is then reloaded. The
toolbar keeps search and `Active | Closed | All` (sent to every server), merges
queues by prefix across servers with summed counts, and adds a `Server` menu
in which an unavailable server is marked and cannot be picked. The agent in
the route never narrows the table. Search,
status, queue and server are kept per session in `tasks:all-view:v1` and the
shared `tasks:queue-filter:v1`. An empty result says **No tasks** with
**Clear filters**. **New task** asks for an agent (labelled with its server)
and a queue of that agent's server, and creates
the task there assigned to that agent. The queue list preselects the queue
saved for that server in `tasks:new-task-queue:v1` when it exists there, and
the created task saves its queue for that server.

Selecting a row opens the task in place in the same detail sheet, loaded from
its own server. There the Assignee field lists every agent on every server as
`agent · server`. Choosing an agent on another server saves any other edits
on the source, then moves the tree with the export and import of
[the server-to-server transfer](/docs/tasks#moving-a-task-to-another-server).
The root is imported unassigned, so an agent of the same name on the target
cannot take it first, and is then assigned by an ordinary update, which sends
the agent its assignment notification; subtasks keep their assignees. The
import's refusals — no queue with that prefix or a taken key — leave the task on its server and are shown as an
error. Once the import succeeds the task lives on the target: if cancelling the
source copy or assigning the agent then fails, the error names the step and
the sheet still follows the task to its new server. A choice whose server
stopped answering between the pick and **Save** is refused rather than written
as an assignee.

Selecting another agent in the sidebar while an agent workspace is open keeps
the tab that is currently open and shows the new agent in it, so the same view
answers the same question about the next agent. An unknown tab still falls back
to Terminal (Tasks in Simple mode), and a selected task in the Tasks query is dropped because it belongs
to the agent being left. Selecting an agent from anywhere else — a
team, or a freshly created agent — still opens Terminal, or Tasks in Simple mode.
Start and Stop live only in the agent header; a stopped agent's Terminal tab says so
without a Start button of its own.

When a known explicit server route temporarily loses its tunnel or its
authoritative aggregate refresh fails, the Desktop retains its last successful
server and agent snapshot in React memory rather than flashing the whole pane
to an error. The live host badge and a local status message identify the
unavailable/reconnecting state; that host's agent controls and cached sidebar
agent rows are read-only until a successful refresh for the same host replaces
the snapshot atomically. Cached data is never persisted or used as an API
target, other server navigation remains available, and a missing host still
fails closed rather than falling back to local authority.

A reconnect never remounts a server page. An SSH host loses its endpoint while
its tunnel reconnects and comes back on a new local port. Neither change is
part of a page's identity: Tasks, Workflows, Stores, Settings and Configuration
keep their loaded data, the open task, filters, scroll position and every
unsaved draft. The route boundary keeps one tree shape and only dims the page
and makes it inert under a single status line. A host object keeps its
identity until one of its fields changes, so the sidebar poll does not
restart page loads.

While the host has no endpoint, background loads are skipped rather than
failed. When the new endpoint arrives, each page re-reads once in place:
the task list, the open task, the agent header, Configuration and Mailbox. A
background read that cannot reach the host (`host_not_ready`,
`network_error`) keeps the last data and shows no toast, because the host
header in the left panel already reports the host as offline with its error.
All tasks keeps an unreachable server's rows for the same filter beside that
server's error. An explicit action such as **Save**, **Create** or **Send**
still reports its failure. Its draft stays in the form, ready to send again
once the host is back. Drafts live in tab memory only and are not queued for
later delivery.

Configuration is one column of blocks in a fixed order: **General** (agent
image, image digest, working directory and, while the agent is stopped,
**Create directory if missing**), **Runtime** (harness, model, effort,
Interactive), **Loop and timeouts** (the scheduling and timeout
fields, including **Schedule** with the daemon's next scheduled start under it,
which follows Save; there is no Loop switch), **Goal**, **Messages**, **Budgets (USD)**, **Environment** (agent
shell script and secrets), and **Retention and cleanup**. Start, Stop and
Restart are actions, not settings: they sit in the page header next to the
master-switch state and apply immediately.

**Schedule** is a builder for the agent's `RRULE` (see
[Schedule](/docs/architecture/iteration-loop#schedule)). You select a mode and fill
in its fields: **None** (no schedule), **Every N minutes / hours**, **Daily**
(one time), **Weekly** (days and one time), **Monthly** (a day of the month or
the last day, and one time), **Once** (a date and a time), or **Custom RRULE**
(a text field for any rule). The builder shows a one-line summary and the rule
it sends. Times are in the time zone of the daemon host, not of the browser.
When the page loads a saved rule, the builder selects the mode that builds
exactly that rule. If no mode does, for example a rule with two times or with
`UNTIL`, it selects **Custom RRULE** and shows the rule unchanged. A rule you
do not edit is not marked **Changed**. When you select another mode, the
builder drops the saved `DTSTART`, and the daemon starts the new rule at the
current minute.

Every editable field of every block belongs to one page-wide draft with one
save mechanic. A field is dirty when its normalized draft differs from the
value last loaded; the field shows **Changed**, its block counts its unsaved
changes, and a sticky bar at the bottom of the page lists the count and the
blocks and offers **Reset** and **Save**. No block has its own save button.
**Reset** drops every draft. **Save** first validates every changed field in
the browser and sends nothing while any is invalid: it shows the field (clearing
a search that hid it) and focuses it. Then it sends only the changed fields,
serially in page order (harness before model and effort), using the existing
per-field endpoints; the four budget limits and the two retention limits are
sent as one request each, as before. It stops at the first failure without
sending the fields after it: acknowledged fields adopt the daemon's canonical
values after a reload, while the failed field (with the server's reason beside
it) and the ones never attempted stay dirty drafts, so the next Save sends only
them. There is no batch endpoint, so a Save is not atomic. Harness and
Interactive are saved with the page like every other field; they take effect the
next time the agent starts and never restart it. **Create directory if
missing** is saved with the working directory as one request: when it is on,
Save sends the path with `create: true`, and the daemon makes a missing
directory before it validates the path. After a successful Save the switch is
off again.

A search box above the blocks filters by block: a case-insensitive match of
every query word against a block's title, description, field labels, helpers
and keywords (for example `cwd`, `tmux`, `dlq`, `usd`) shows that whole block
and highlights the matching fields. **Changed only** shows just the blocks with
unsaved changes. Block chips jump to a block and show its change count. Search
only hides blocks; drafts in hidden blocks are kept and are still saved.

For a stopped agent, the working directory is edited with the selected host's
directory autocomplete. Saving changes the CWD used by the next launch; it does
not move files or start, stop, or restart the agent. Active agents show the
current CWD read-only until they are stopped. Remote agent reads, directory
suggestions, and saves all use the host identified by the agent route rather
than whichever daemon was previously active. Refreshing live agent, image or
host status does not replace an unsaved draft; the draft is discarded only when
the agent or the host changes. The agent image is a draft field too; **Copy
digest**, **Cancel pending** and **Retry** of a failed pending assignment stay
immediate actions in an actions row that says they are not part of Save.

Model and effort use the same grouped suggestions as agent creation, for the
agent's host and the selected harness.

The Loop section also exposes the positive **AI inactivity timeout** in seconds,
defaulting to 1800 (30 minutes) per agent. When a running iteration exceeds it without an
attributed AI-proxy request, the daemon reports `state=error`, which the agent header
shows. The controls remain enabled because this
signal does not stop the loop or iteration; the next request restores
`state=running`. Ordinary creation starts at 1800 seconds, while Clone preserves
the source agent's configured value.

The **Messages** block uses that same draft contract for the
positive whole-number `messages_batch` and `messages_max_queue` fields.
New-agent drafts use a maximum queue of 100, while Clone keeps the source
agent's configured value.

Configuration also renders the daemon-authoritative per-agent USD budget
projection. Its four calendar rows pair each current spend with one editable
limit (spent beside the limit), label zero as Unlimited, and save in one
request against the explicit agent-route host. Older daemons that omit the
projection get no Budgets block. The agent header and sidebar use the same
projection; they show an explicit Out of budget state and every exhausted
period rather than recomputing spend in the browser. Older daemons simply omit
the additive projection.

The workspace header also consumes daemon-authoritative message status. When
`messages_queue_full` is true it displays
**Message queue full: pending / limit** in destructive styling; it never
recomputes queue state in the browser. The normal three-second status refresh
removes the indicator after processing or clearing lowers the queue.

When the daemon reports a halt reason for the agent, the workspace header shows
it under the identity line, so a loop that stopped before any iteration existed
— a failed image activation, for example — is visible on every tab. It is toned
as an error for an `error` halt and neutrally for an `idle_limit` one, and falls
back to `error_reason` when the daemon reports one without a halt. The line is
not gated on whether the agent is started, because a stop-policy, idle-limit or
launch-failure reason matters exactly when the loop is off. When there is no reason, nothing
extra is rendered at all — no empty element and no placeholder.

The common agent list can be hidden and restored throughout the hierarchy. On macOS the
main Tauri window retains native traffic lights under an overlay titlebar, and
the sidebar icon is immediately after their reserved area in the global
toolbar. The application-settings action and theme icon are the other titlebar
controls. Empty toolbar space is draggable, while daemon status banners remain
below the titlebar so they never cover the native controls. The shared
persisted sidebar state drives both that control and the server/agent shell. Its
width and hidden state persist in the WebView localStorage record
`terminals:sidebar:v1`; the first read after upgrading adopts the sidebar saved by
the removed terminal canvas under `terminals:workspace:v1`. The 72px gap kept
for the traffic lights exists only in the Desktop app.

### Compact screens

Below 1024 CSS pixels (Tailwind's `lg`) the window is compact: phones and
most tablets. Below 768 CSS pixels (Tailwind's `md`, the `DRAWER_QUERY` of
`useMediaQuery`) the agent list takes no room beside the island. The
titlebar's sidebar toggle becomes a **Open menu** button that opens the same
list as a drawer from the left, at most 85% of the width. The drawer opens
without focus in **Search agents**, so a phone does not raise its keyboard;
the first Tab moves focus into it. From 768 to 1023 CSS pixels the agent list
stays a column, and the titlebar's **Hide agents** / **Show agents** toggle
collapses it as on a wide window, saved in `terminals:sidebar:v1`. Picking an agent, a server or a team, **New agent**,
**Add server**, editing a server or cloning an agent closes it, and so do a tap
outside, Escape, and any route change, Back included: the drawer belongs to the
history entry it opened on. A window that grows past 768 CSS pixels drops it, so
it does not come back when the tablet turns again. It has no resize handle and
is never stored:
the wide layout's width and hidden state in `terminals:sidebar:v1` stay as
they were.

Other compact rules:

- The agent header wraps instead of overflowing. The image and runtime badges
  truncate with the full value in their tooltip, and the Exec / Start or Stop /
  Kill / menu cluster takes a row of its own under the identity, so it never
  covers it.
- The agent tabs, the server context bar and the Settings navigation scroll
  sideways with no visible bar, and the current tab scrolls into view. The
  Settings navigation is a strip above the page instead of a column.
- Below 640 CSS pixels (`sm`) the workspace switcher shows its icon only, the
  task table shows only `Key`, `Task` and `Status` at fixed widths, and the
  Columns menu, the column move grips and the resize handles are hidden. The
  saved column
  layout `tasks:columns:v1` is not changed; priority stays in the task's
  detail.
- Dialogs keep a 16px margin on each side, and two-column dialogs and editors
  (the workspace manager, the image source editor) stack.

`ui/tests/responsive.pw.ts` checks these at 360×800, 390×844, 820×1180 and
1180×820 against an isolated daemon: no visible element may end past the right
edge of the window unless it is inside its own horizontal scroller, the header
controls must not cover the agent's details, and the agent list must be a
drawer exactly when the window is compact.

**Send files**, Attach, and terminal file drops all upload through the selected
server's streaming `PUT /api/files/raw` endpoint, with a 1 GiB per-file limit.
The browser sends each `File` as the raw request body instead of building a
base64/JSON copy. Uploads have no agent destination: files live in the server's
shared files directory and the returned absolute paths are inserted into the
corresponding draft or reported when no terminal is available. Terminal retains
its explicit host target.

The agent Terminal tab mounts xterm.js and opens
`GET /api/agents/{name}/terminal`. Binary WebSocket frames carry PTY bytes;
text frames carry resize messages. A host or agent route change tears down the
old socket and dials the newly selected target without stopping the tmux
session.

In the Terminal tab, explicit `http://` and `https://` text in terminal
output opens in the operator's default browser on **Command-click** (the `Meta`
modifier); this is a Desktop capability and does nothing in a plain browser.
The Android app has no Command key, so there a tap on the link opens it. An
ordinary click never opens anything and keeps xterm's own focus, selection and
mouse behaviour untouched. Nothing else is actionable: file paths, `file://`,
`javascript:`, `data:`, custom schemes, protocol-relative and bare-host text are
not even rendered as links, and the URL is parsed and its scheme re-checked
natively before anything is launched — the terminal matcher and the WebView are
not the authorization boundary. A link that cannot be opened reports a fixed
message that never contains the terminal line.

The Terminal tab toolbar exposes **Scrollback**. It sends tmux's own
copy-mode entry sequence (prefix `C-b`, then `[`) over the existing byte socket, and the toolbar then shows a persistent
**Viewing scrollback** status, **Page back** / **Page forward** controls, and an
**Exit scrollback** button. Live keystrokes are paused while tmux is in
copy-mode; press `q` in the focused terminal or use **Exit scrollback** to
return to live output. Every control is a labelled button reachable by keyboard.
Because the browser has no authoritative tmux mode event, the status describes
the state Tariboy *requested*, not a verified tmux mode, and it is cleared
whenever `q` is typed in the terminal, **Exit scrollback** is used, the socket
closes, the terminal identity changes, the session becomes absent, or the tile
unmounts — leaving copy-mode any other way still strands the status, notably via
`Escape`, which cancels under tmux's default emacs table (including from the
toolbar's own **Esc** hotkey) but only clears the selection under `copy-mode-vi`,
so the browser cannot infer it. Entering and leaving scrollback are both
announced through a status region that stays in the DOM either way — a live
region that unmounts announces nothing — and leaving via **Exit scrollback**
returns keyboard focus to the **Scrollback** control, while leaving with `q`
keeps focus in the terminal. tmux mouse reporting stays off, so wheel and drag input continue to
belong to the inner harness TUI.

What Scrollback browses is the tmux **pane history**, not xterm scrollback, and
it is bounded: the shim sets each managed session's `history-limit` to 10,000
lines (tmux's own default is 2,000), so older output is discarded by tmux and
cannot be recovered from the browser. Nothing about the history is persisted by
the UI.

The agent header exposes manual **Exec** before Start/Stop, only while the
agent is enabled and not `bare:latest`, for interactive and non-interactive
agents alike. It opens a dialog whose optional, memory-only one-shot text is
sent to the route-selected host and affects only the newly requested iteration.
Exec does not start the agent or persist the draft. A successful request closes
the dialog and, when the Terminal tab shows an interactive terminal, reconnects its
startup handling; a rejected request keeps the dialog and the draft for retry.

Permanent agent deletion requires confirmation in an in-app dialog that names
the agent and warns that its durable data is also removed. Confirm sends the
existing `force=true` and `purge=true` request. While that request is pending,
the dialog cannot be dismissed or submitted again. The Terminal tab returns home
only after success; on failure it keeps the dialog open, restores its controls,
and reports the error so the operator can retry. **Kill session** remains a
separate action with its existing browser confirmation and does not delete the
agent or its durable data.

An agent's **Retention and cleanup** block edits that agent's override of the
server-wide iteration defaults with the page Save: each field shows
`0 = server default (N)`, and the block lists the effective limits and that
pruned iterations are archived with their database rows first.

Secrets in the Environment block are write-only. The block lists key names
only. Removing a key and adding a key and value are page drafts applied by
Save: a removal is shown as **Will be removed** until then, and a new value
lives only in tab memory, is sent in a POST body and never in a URL, is never
rendered, and is cleared once the daemon acknowledges it.

**Preview cleanup** and **Prune now** stay immediate actions outside Save.
The in-app retention prune is guarded by a confirmation dialog that names
the operation as permanently destructive and bounds it to the current
retention policy. Confirming dismisses the dialog and issues the real,
non-dry-run prune; while it is in flight the destructive action is disabled
and cannot be issued twice. A failure is reported beside that action inside
the bounded destructive section, not in the dialog, so the operator can
read it and retry. Previewing what the policy would remove stays a
separate, unconfirmed action.

Terminal connection outcomes are intentionally distinct:

- `4404` is retried for a five-second startup grace because the agent engine and
  shim socket can become ready shortly after Start returns;
- `1000/eof` means the attached PTY ended and stops immediately;
- abnormal transport closes retry with capped exponential delay while the view
  remains mounted.

The Desktop SSH host dialog also keeps transport connectivity separate from
the result of the current provision or update operation. It maps native phases
into six ordered user-facing steps and retains a failed update result even if
rollback restores a healthy old tunnel. Native stdout and stderr events are
bounded diagnostic output, not lifecycle results; only an explicit error event
or a failed host runtime state terminates the operation. Raw process output is
collapsed under **Technical details**, while the main flow renders one
actionable error and one primary next action.

`DaemonProvider` also exposes `daemon_status.app_version` to both host-list
surfaces. Their compact Update action is derived only from a confirmed mismatch
between that bundle version and the non-empty persisted/runtime remote daemon
version. Unknown versions fail closed without an update indicator; the host
editor retains its explicit manual update action.

See [Development](/docs/development#react-ui) for source and generated-artifact
verification.

---

# Autopilot
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/tariboy/autopilot

Autopilot is the daemon-controlled iteration loop of a started agent. An agent
has one on/off switch: **Start** turns the whole agent on (iterations, messages,
Goal, and the interactive Terminal), and **Stop** turns all of it off. There is
no separate Autopilot switch.

Agents from the terminal-only `bare:latest` image never run autonomous
iterations. To keep a non-bare agent from iterating on a timer, set its
interval to 0; it then iterates only for messages, including Goal tasks.

## Trigger model

While the agent is started, an iteration can start from:

- a configured timer interval; or
- an open letter in the agent's inbox, including a `task.goal` letter.

Letters are durable. Sending a letter to the agent stores it in its inbox and
nudges the loop. The runner includes the open letters in the next prompt. A
request stays open until the agent replies to it; a notice closes when the
iteration finishes normally. Harness errors, timeouts, and kills leave both
open for bounded redelivery.

Stopping the agent prevents new scheduled and message-triggered iterations. It
does not delete open letters.

A stop policy (`on_timeout=stop` or `on_error=stop`) halts the loop with an
error reason. The agent stays started and shows the `error` state. Start it
again to clear the reason and resume the loop.

## Configure conservatively

Start with:

- an image prompt that defines one coherent unit of work;
- a long enough interval to inspect outcomes;
- a soft timeout that fits normal work;
- a hard timeout that bounds the worst case;
- a low cost budget;
- no external plugins sending mail until the timer path is understood.

Set the interval and timeouts in **Configuration → Loop and timeouts**, or in
the **Loop** section of the create dialog. Activity shows trigger,
iteration state, result, deadlines, audit, usage, and cost. For Claude and
Codex harnesses, the audit is presented as a readable timeline of messages,
reasoning, commands, skills, tool calls, and results; model and token metadata
remains available on each AI call. A running soft deadline may be extended only
before timeout enforcement starts.

## Controls

- **Start / Stop** (agent header) — turn the agent on or off. From the CLI use
  `tariboy agent start NAME` and `tariboy agent stop NAME`.
- **Exec** (agent header, shown while the agent is enabled) — start one manual
  iteration immediately. It is available for both interactive and
  non-interactive agents; optional one-shot text, entered in its dialog, is
  appended only to that iteration's assembled prompt.
- **Kill** — immediately stop current iteration or session; use when work is
  unsafe or stuck.
- **Budget** — reject AI calls once the configured spend limit is reached.
- **Audit** — inspect each proxied AI request and tool timeline. Copy readable
  Markdown or export a ZIP for the selected iteration or all retained
  iterations. Exports contain sensitive agent data; review the warning before
  downloading them.

After a kill, verify the Activity outcome and the agent's open letters before
starting the agent again. A killed or failed iteration leaves its letters
open for redelivery.

## Event-driven progression

Mail is the layer behind message triggers. It lets agents, plugins, schedules
and scripts wake work without polling. Begin with one sender writing to one
agent, then add groups after the single-agent letter lifecycle is understood.

Read an agent's inbox, sent letters and archive, with its dead letters, with
`tariboy mail inbox --as agent:NAME`, `sent` and `archive`.

See [Mailbox architecture](/docs/architecture/messaging) and the [Mail
reference](/docs/reference/mail) for the complete contract.

---

# Binaries & commands
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/tariboy/binaries

Six real binaries are built by `make build`:

| Binary | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `tariboyd` | The [daemon](/docs/architecture) — long-running, owns all durable state. |
| `tariboy` | The [operator CLI](/docs/binaries/operator-cli) — human/CI client over the socket. |
| `tariboy-tasks` | The Native Tasks client; installers also provide its `ttasks` alias. |
| `tariboy-mail` | The [mail client](/docs/reference/mail); installers also provide its `tmail` alias. |
| `tariboy-shim` | Runs [one harness iteration under a watchdog](/docs/architecture/shim). |
| `tariboy-store` | A standalone [image registry](/docs/binaries/store) server. |
| `tariboy-plugin-telegram` | The bundled Telegram mail and operator-surface plugin. |

The daemon installs or refreshes the Telegram plugin from its sibling binary at
startup. Optional external plugins are built and distributed independently.

`make build` does not embed agent image sources or skills. Register a Store such
as the `tariboy` Store (**Add tariboy Store** on the Stores page, or
`tariboy store add tariboy https://github.com/alekzonder/tariboy-store.git`)
and build the desired image on each daemon that needs it. The daemon synthesizes only the
reserved empty `bare:latest` image.

## Client/daemon version drift

`tariboy` and the [agent tool scripts](/docs/binaries/agent-tools) read the
`X-Tariboy-Version` header the daemon stamps on
[every response](/docs/architecture#version-reporting). When that version differs
from the client's own build, the client prints a warning naming both versions and
its own path, strictly on **stderr**. It does not
change stdout or the exit code, so output parsing is unaffected. A daemon old
enough to send no header produces no warning.

This matters because packaged skill scripts and the agent `tasks` / `i-am-done`
compatibility shims execute from the active image bridge: without the warning,
a script too old to know a newer flag looks like it simply did nothing.
`scripts/whoami.sh` prints both `client_version` and `daemon_version` for exactly this
reason — it is the first command to run when the tools behave strangely.

The authoritative operator command list is generated from the binary
(`tariboy --help-json`) and documented in the
[command reference](/docs/reference/commands).

Queue agent pools and triggers are configured with the operator `ttasks` client
or operator REST, and pools also through [`tariboy compose`](/docs/binaries/compose).
Workflow images are built and stored with `tariboy workflow`; see
[Workflow images](/docs/workflow-images) and
[Task workflows](/docs/task-workflows).

## The three command surfaces

<CardGroup>
  <Card title="Operator commands" href="/docs/binaries/operator-cli" icon="user-cog">
    `tariboy <group> <command>` — run by a human or CI against the daemon.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Agent capability scripts" href="/docs/binaries/agent-tools" icon="wrench">
    Packaged skill-local scripts — run *inside* an agent over its per-agent socket.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Native Tasks" href="/docs/tasks" icon="list-tree">
    `ttasks <verb>` — Native Tasks for operators and identity-bound agents.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

---

# Agent capability scripts
Source: https://alekzonder.github.io/tariboy/binaries/agent-tools

Run **inside** an agent from the applicable packaged skill directory. Each
`scripts/*.sh` launcher executes the skill's Python 3 standard-library client.
Only the legacy `tasks` and `i-am-done` also have PATH compatibility shims. The scripts
talk to the identity-bound per-agent socket selected by
`$TARIBOY_TOOLS_SOCKET`; the daemon derives the agent identity server-side.
For non-bare iterations, `python3` is resolved to an absolute path from the
final agent environment before the harness starts. An explicit agent `PATH`
must therefore include it.

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `scripts/whoami.sh` | agent, cwd, current iteration |
| `scripts/status.sh [set …]` | read / set the one-line status |
| `scripts/loop.sh done` | finish this iteration (`i-am-done`) |
| `scripts/context.sh get` / `set <text>` | read / overwrite durable working memory |
| `scripts/goal.sh set <TASK-KEY>` | select an assigned active Goal for this iteration |
| `tmail inbox`/`sent`/`archive`/`show` | read the mailbox |
| `tmail send --to P …` / `tmail reply ID TEXT` | send a letter, answer one |
| `scripts/schedule.sh add`/`ls`/`cancel` | agent-owned scheduled wake-ups |
| `scripts/scripts.sh run`/`schedule`/`rerun`/`ls`/`runs`/`logs`/`cancel`/`rm` | local asynchronous commands and run history |
| `GET /tools/group/info`, `status`, `observe/{member}`, `POST /tools/group/loop` | group coordination; group sends are `tmail send --to group:<g>` or `agent:<member>` |

`tariboy-tasks` is installed globally with the `ttasks` alias. Packaged daemons
also expose it through a shared runtime `bin/ttasks` symlink on their baseline
`PATH`, so fresh Desktop agents can use it before optional CLI installation.
An explicit agent `PATH` override must retain that directory or another
installed `ttasks`. A non-empty
`TARIBOY_TOOLS_SOCKET` selects its identity-bound agent mode and a missing or
unreachable socket fails closed; without the variable it uses the host Unix
daemon socket as the customer actor. Images that enable `plugins: [{name:
tasks}]` also get the bare `tasks` legacy compatibility shim. See [Native
Tasks](/docs/tasks) for the command flow.

On a task that follows a queue's [workflow](/docs/task-workflows) the daemon
assigns the work, and `ttasks done`, `ttasks update --status`, and
`ttasks ready --claim` do not apply. The agent reads `ttasks workflow get KEY`,
sets declared artifacts with `ttasks artifacts set|ls|show`, and leaves its
status with `ttasks advance KEY --outcome NAME --from STATUS`, where `--from`
makes a retried advance fail with `status_changed` instead of applying twice.
`advance` waits for the transition's check scripts and exits non-zero on a
rejection or failure, naming the next command; `--no-wait` returns the pending
request at once. `ttasks workflow runs KEY` and `ttasks workflow log KEY RUN`
show what the scripts did. `ttasks workflow move`, `ttasks cancel`, `ttasks requeue`, and the
`ttasks queue` commands are operator-only. Workflow scripts themselves never
receive the tools socket.

`tariboyd` normally selects and persists one sticky assigned task per enabled
agent, then stamps its key and top-level root onto the AI-proxy lease before the
harness starts. If an iteration starts without a task, the agent may create or
claim one through `ttasks` and run `scripts/goal.sh set <TASK-KEY>`. The task
must be active and assigned to that agent. Subsequent requests use the new
task/root attribution; earlier requests remain unattributed. A second call with
a different key is rejected.

Task priority is one of `P0` (Critical), `P1` (High), `P2` (Normal), or `P3`
(Low). New tasks default to `P2`; set or change it explicitly with:

```bash
ttasks create --queue OPS --title "Restore service" --priority P0
ttasks update OPS-12 --priority P1
```

`ttasks show`, list commands, and `--json` output include `priority`. Roots and
